opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so what's striking to me is that you'd naively expect a two-layer attention-only Transformer trained on natural language to be doing something pretty simple. It learns bigram statistics, then maybe some n-gram statistics, then forms an induction circuit, and that's roughly the story. When you look more carefully, though, there's a lot more going on.

The multigram circuit is the machinery the model uses to predict tokens based on these longer, more flexible patterns. Not just "token A follows token B," but combinations of tokens that can be spread out across the context and don't have to be strictly contiguous. What I find sophisticated is how the model ends up implementing this. It isn't one head doing one job. The computation is distributed across both layers, with heads in the first layer and the second layer coordinating. Some components are essentially building up representations of which tokens have appeared, and later components read those off to make predictions. There's a real compositional structure there.

The other thing that's interesting, from our perspective of studying development, is how this circuit forms over training and how it interacts with the induction circuit. You see these two mechanisms competing for and sharing the same limited resources, the same heads, the same subspaces. The model has to work out how to fit both into a very small network. Some of the structure it builds early on seems to get repurposed or reorganized later. So you get this picture where even a tiny model goes through a fairly rich developmental trajectory, with transient structure that appears and then gets partially dismantled.

For me, that's the exciting part. It suggests that even in these toy settings, the "simple" algorithms we tell ourselves models are learning are really cartoons. If we want to understand larger models, we need tools that can track this kind of distributed, evolving computation, and not just find a single clean circuit at the end of training. That's part of why we've been leaning on tools from singular learning theory, like the local learning coefficient and its refinements, to detect when these changes happen and which components are involved.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the thing that I find sophisticated about it is that it's not really one circuit, it's this whole layered structure that the model builds up over the course of training, and it ends up looking a lot more like an induction head than you'd expect from the name.

So let me back up a bit. The basic observation is that if you train a two-layer attention-only transformer on natural language, one of the things it has to learn is just statistics of the data. The simplest version is bigrams: given the current token, what's the next token likely to be? And that's something a zero-layer model can do, it's just an embedding-unembedding lookup. But then there are trigrams, and four-grams, and so on, where the prediction depends on the previous few tokens. And the model can learn those too, but it has to use attention to do it, because the information about the previous tokens has to get moved to the current position somehow.

And what's sophisticated is how it does that. You'd naively think, okay, there's a previous-token head, it copies the previous token forward, and now the MLP or the unembedding can do a trigram lookup. But what we actually see is that the model is doing something much more like compression. It's not storing a giant table of n-grams. It's learning these "skip-grams" and "multigrams" where the context is more like a bag of relevant tokens at various offsets, and it's superimposing a lot of these on top of each other. So one head might be contributing to thousands of different n-gram-like predictions at once, and the way it does that is by exploiting the geometry of the residual stream really aggressively.

The other thing that I think is genuinely surprising is the developmental story. If you watch this form over training, it's not that the model just learns bigrams, then trigrams, then four-grams in order. There are these discrete stages, and you can see them in the loss curve and in the local learning coefficient, where the model is restructuring how it represents the context. Early on it's doing something pretty crude, almost positional. Then there's a transition where it starts using the actual content of the previous tokens. And then later you get the induction circuit forming, which is in some sense the limit of this process: instead of memorizing which token follows which n-gram, it learns the general rule of "look back for where this happened before and copy what came next."

So the multigram circuit is kind of the memorization side of that story, and induction is the generalization side, and they're competing for the same capacity in the model. I think that tension, between a circuit that's basically a very clever lookup table and a circuit that's implementing an algorithm, is one of the clearest examples we have of what "the model learning structure" actually looks like at the level of mechanism. And it's small enough that you can actually track it, which is the whole reason we care about these toy models in the first place.

astra-6.text:
What I find sophisticated is that it’s not just memorizing a table of n-gram statistics. It can compose those statistics. One attention head can pick out a relevant piece of context, and a head in the next layer can use that information to decide what to attend to. So the thing being matched is itself something the network has computed.

That lets you get patterns that are more flexible than contiguous sequences of tokens—patterns with gaps, or with different parts of the context contributing to the prediction. And all of this is happening in just two layers. It’s a nice example of how something that sounds very simple, like learning n-grams, can conceal quite a rich computational mechanism.

r001.rationale: The response describes two-layer composition and flexible context patterns, but does not state that layer coordination appears necessary for nested parenthesis matching.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find sophisticated is that it’s doing something more general than just matching a fixed sequence of tokens. With an ordinary induction head, the picture is: you’ve seen A followed by B, you see A again, and you predict B. But often a single token isn’t enough to identify the relevant context. You need to match a sequence.

The multigram circuit can use the first layer to put information about preceding tokens into the representation at a position. Then the second layer can compare those contextualized representations. So it’s effectively matching longer chunks, even though it only has two layers to work with.

And I think that’s a nice example of why the depth of a model doesn’t straightforwardly tell you how sophisticated its computation is. A lot can happen through the composition of attention heads and the information they write into the residual stream.
